doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: LP groove quality and putting strong cuts first
summary: Conniff explains inner grooves sound poorer, so the first bands were most important; tape speed is also touched on.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah. Like you’ll have a watch — this is a second hand and like if I was here and I got a great idea and I said, “do you mind if we stop the tape a minute” I can sing myself eight bars and stop it, and say okay let’s go on, and I can go home and I can remember the song and what the tempo was by the eight bars. Yeah I would time everything out, and would shoot for around — well I didn’t make it a real rule, you know, because you always had some songs in there that you put in there for airplay. I remember on the album of “Broadway and Rhythms,” “On the Street Where you Live” was almost 2:10, something about like 2:10, and I got a lot of airplay on that. So that was the cut in that album. I knew the guys would play that cut out of the album, because everybody liked that. So I didn’t worry too much, maybe another one could be up around three. Another thing, I wonder if the people that might hear this might be interested in knowing, we don’t have an album in here, but in the middle of this album, when you’re playing an album, when the needle’s out here, the revolutions of the record player in those days is always the same, 33-1/3 revolutions per minute. So when the needle is out here, it’s going around this big long circumference. When it’s in here, it’s going a very short distance in the same period of time. The quality is much poorer here. The quality is three times as good out here as it is here. And we had to think about that, in the timing of the album, how far apart the grooves were, and how far we would go in here. Because you’d get to a certain point here, and the quality got so poor in there that you didn’t want to use it anymore.
We don’t have that problem with CDs and numbers and digital and all of that.
Yeah. And it relates to tape speed too. When if you tape something—

No tape speed is determined what’s going across the heads. It’s pulled through the heads by the rollers. Well actually the reel is going faster or slower, but the speed of the tape through the heads is always the same.
15 IPS we used to record, and now we double it.
Did that idea of the songs that are in the middle of the record, might not sound quite as good, did that determine what arrangements you might put in there?
Not so much as the first band would determine. You figure when a disc jockey got a new album, or they used to let people go in the record stores and play and listen, you figured

people were going to listen to the first band and maybe skip to the second. We always thought those were the most important bands. That if they liked the first couple of bands they’d buy the album or they’d put it on the air. So those were the ones. We didn’t pay too much attention to the inner bands because we knew the quality wasn’t as good anyway.
Wow. I never thought of that.
I don’t know if other artists — maybe other artists never thought of those things. But I was very commercial and looked at all aspects of the business. I got into the covers and everything.
